strengths: Innovative formulation of sparse-view CT (SVCT) reconstruction using neural operators (specifically Discrete-Continuous Convolutions - DISCO), allowing a single model to natively handle multi-rate sampling and arbitrary image resolutions without retraining.

Strong integration of CT-specific physics and geometry into the network architecture, including: (1) dual-domain processing in both sinogram and image spaces, (2) a dual-branch sinogram operator that utilizes the Fourier slice theorem to capture complementary spatial-frequency features, and (3) a rotation-equivariant design using a modified circular padding scheme to respect the symmetries of tomographic acquisition.

Excellent experimental results demonstrating substantial gains (over 3dB PSNR) against multiple competitive baselines including unrolled CNNs, transformers, and diffusion-based methods (while being 500x faster than the latter at inference time).

Strong evidence of the continuous-space advantages via successful zero-shot super-resolution in both the image and sinogram domains, as well as robust out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across noisy sinograms and different datasets.
weaknesses: The rotation-equivariance mathematical formulations (such as the $\pi$-periodicity-with-flip symmetry) assume a parallel-beam geometry. However, for the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset, a fan-beam geometry is used. The paper does not fully clarify how rotation-equivariance holds up or degrades under fan-beam geometry, where simple translation in the sinogram does not correspond exactly to image rotation without re-binning.

The unrolled network (Eqn. 4) relies on the forward projector $\mathcal{A}$ and its adjoint $\mathcal{A}^*$. While DISCO handles the resolution-agnostic learned priors, the projection operators are inherently discrete in practice. It remains slightly unclear how the varying discretization of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}^*$ across different sampling rates affects the discretization-convergence guarantees of the overall unrolled framework.

The paper lacks details on the computational overhead of training with DISCO due to the repeated kernel sampling, though the authors do specify that inference-time complexity is identical to standard CNNs once the kernels are discretized.

strengths: Pioneering application of Neural Operators (specifically Discrete-Continuous Convolutions / DISCO) to sparse-view CT reconstruction, offering a elegant solution to the multi-rate and multi-resolution clinical generalization problem.

Well-motivated, domain-specific designs: the dual-branch sinogram operator ($NO_{s,spatial}$ and $NO_{s,freq}$) mimics the spatial-frequency properties of Filtered Back Projection, and the flipped circular padding scheme elegantly enforces the physical $\pi$-periodicity-with-flip symmetry of parallel-beam tomographic acquisition.

Strong empirical results across multiple clinical datasets (AAPM and Kidney CT) demonstrating substantial gains (+3.4dB PSNR) over equivalent discrete CNN baselines, as well as outstanding zero-shot super-resolution performance.
Excellent analysis of computational complexity, showing that the continuous kernels can be pre-discretized at inference time, resulting in zero extra runtime overhead compared to standard CNNs.

Comprehensive supplementary material that includes detailed mathematical proofs for rotation-equivariance, thorough hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and out-of-distribution robustness assessments.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to 2D parallel-beam and fan-beam CT geometries. In practice, clinical CT is predominantly 3D (cone-beam or helical). A discussion of the practical challenges, mathematical formulations, and scaling behavior when extending the proposed 2D DISCO to 3D Radon operators would strengthen the paper.

It is not fully clear how the physical data consistency layers ($\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}^*$) adapt when the image resolution or sinogram sampling grid changes. While the Neural Operator handles arbitrary coordinate queries, the discrete Radon and backprojection matrices are resolution-dependent; further details on how the system scales these physical operators dynamically would improve clarity.

Minor formatting and presentation omissions, such as a missing placeholder link for the code repository in the abstract ("Our code is available at .") and occasional inconsistent subscript formatting for the operators ($NO_s$ vs. $NO_s$, $NO_i$ vs. $NO_i$) in the main text.

strengths: This paper presents the first application of Neural Operators (specifically Discrete-Continuous Convolutions or DISCO) to sparse-view CT, successfully addressing the limitation of traditional CNNs which are bound to specific discretization grids.

The proposed dual-domain architecture elegantly leverages CT physics: the sinogram-space operator ($NO_s$) operates in polar coordinates to enforce rotation equivariance, while incorporating a joint spatial-frequency design inspired by the Fourier Slice Theorem and Filtered Back Projection.

The rotation-equivariant design is mathematically rigorous and highly practical, utilizing a flipped circular padding scheme that explicitly respects the physical $\pi$-periodicity-with-flip symmetry of parallel-beam CT acquisition.

Strong empirical performance across multiple distinct datasets (AAPM Low-Dose, Kidney CT, LIDC-IDRI) showing substantial gains (>3.4dB PSNR) over standard unrolled CNNs and other baselines in both multi-rate and zero-shot super-resolution settings.
Incredibly fast inference speed compared to state-of-the-art diffusion models (>500x faster) while maintaining comparable or better reconstruction fidelity.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, thoroughly ablated (including studies on spatial vs. frequency branches, circular padding, hyperparameter sensitivity, and complexity analysis), and very clearly presented.
weaknesses: The method is evaluated primarily on 2D parallel-beam and fan-beam CT geometries. While the paper mentions extending this to 3D CT as future work, clinical CT is dominantly 3D cone-beam or helical CT, where implementing continuous neural operators is significantly more complex.

Although inference is computationally efficient because the continuous kernels are pre-discretized, training requires continuous integration and kernel sampling at each forward pass, incurring a 20% to 42% increase in FLOPs. This training overhead could be discussed more prominently.

The unrolled framework's dependency on exact forward and adjoint operators ($A$ and $A^*$) means any clinical application with physical motion or alignment errors might violate the assumed physics, which is a common limitation for model-based unrolled networks that could be explicitly acknowledged.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and mathematically elegant formulation of sparse-view CT reconstruction in the continuous function space using Neural Operators (DISCO), allowing the network to be resolution- and sampling-rate agnostic.
The integration of physical priors and rotational equivariance into the polar-coordinate sinogram space through a customized flipped circular padding scheme is highly clever and physically sound.
The joint spatial-frequency learning architecture in the sinogram domain (inspired by the Fourier slice theorem and classical Filtered Backprojection) is an intuitive and effective design choice.

The experimental evaluation is extensive, demonstrating substantial performance improvements (3-4 dB PSNR) over strong baselines (including CNNs, Transformers, and diffusion models) across multiple view settings, while maintaining high computational efficiency during inference.
weaknesses: The mathematical derivation and implementation of rotational equivariance and the flipped circular padding scheme (Equations 8, 10, 15) strictly assume a parallel-beam geometry. However, the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset utilizes fan-beam geometry (as noted in Section B.1). The authors do not discuss how this parallel-beam-based symmetry behaves or affects reconstruction quality under fan-beam geometry.

The 'Unrolled CNN' baseline is described in Section B.2.2 as operating 'entirely in the image space and does not apply any learned processing in the sinogram domain'. This makes it a somewhat unfair ablation comparison for assessing the benefit of DISCO over standard convolutions. A more direct baseline would be a dual-domain CNN that processes both the sinogram and image domains using standard 2D convolutions.

Although the framework is conceptually continuous and resolution-independent, the zero-shot super-resolution experiments are restricted to a single scale change (e.g., 256x256 to 512x512, and 72-view to 144-view). Evaluating on continuous, non-integer resolutions or irregular/non-uniform view-angle samplings would demonstrate the true generalization capability of the neural operator.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and well-motivated clinical challenge: the generalization of deep learning-based CT reconstruction across varying sampling rates and image resolutions without retraining.

Successfully integrates domain-specific physics and symmetries, such as defining the sinogram operator in natural polar coordinates and enforcing rotational equivariance through a flipped circular padding scheme that respects parallel-beam geometry.
Introduces an elegant joint spatial-frequency sinogram learning framework inspired by the Fourier Slice Theorem and classical Filtered Back Projection (FBP) to capture both local and global features.

Demonstrates strong empirical performance on standard datasets, significantly outperforming unrolled CNNs, transformers (DuDoTrans), and diffusion models (DPS, ALD) in reconstruction quality while running hundreds of times faster than diffusion-based solvers.
Provides compelling evidence of zero-shot super-resolution capabilities in both image and sinogram domains, validating the resolution-agnostic nature of the proposed neural operator framework.
weaknesses: The rotational equivariance derivation and flipped circular padding scheme are theoretically formulated for parallel-beam CT. Since clinical setups predominantly use fan-beam or cone-beam geometries (and fan-beam is used for the AAPM dataset), a more detailed discussion or theoretical analysis is needed to explain how well these parallel-beam assumptions and symmetries generalize to fan-beam configurations.

While the choice of discrete-continuous convolution (DISCO) is well-motivated, the paper lacks a comparison with other popular neural operator architectures (such as the Fourier Neural Operator, FNO) to empirically justify the superiority of DISCO for this task.
The manuscript lacks a detailed breakdown of model complexity, such as parameter counts, training times, and computational costs (GFLOPs) for both the proposed model and the matching-size baselines.

strengths: Strong Motivation & Practical Relevance: Addressing discretization and sampling-rate binding is a major step toward making deep-learning-based CT reconstruction clinically practical, as scanner protocols and resolutions frequently vary.

Principled Architecture Design: The integration of discrete-continuous convolutions (DISCO) into a dual-domain (sinogram and image space) unrolled network is well-designed. The custom adaptations for CT—such as the rotation-equivariant sinogram operator with flipped circular padding and the joint spatial-frequency branches—are physically and mathematically well-justified.

Outstanding Empirical Results: CTO consistently and significantly outperforms robust baselines (including CNNs, transformers, and diffusion models) across different view settings (9, 18, 36, 72 views) on two public datasets.
Zero-Shot Generalization Capabilities: The paper successfully demonstrates zero-shot super-resolution in both the image and sinogram domains, highlighting the benefits of learning in function space.
Thorough Ablation Studies: Well-structured experiments validate the design choices of the frequency-space learning configurations and the rotational equivariance padding mechanism.
weaknesses: Incremental Architectural Novelty: The core building blocks, such as DISCO convolutions and UDNO, are inherited from previous works. The contribution lies primarily in their application and specific domain adaptations to CT reconstruction.

Lack of Computational Complexity Comparison with Single-Pass Baselines: While Table 2 compares inference times with learning-free and diffusion methods, it does not include single-pass deep learning baselines like DuDoTrans, GloReDi, or Unrolled CNN. Providing the parameter counts and inference times for these baselines would clarify if there is any computational overhead associated with the DISCO operator.

Implementation Details of the Forward Projector at Different Resolutions: It is not entirely clear how the forward operator and its adjoint are scaled when the input/output resolutions change. Since the unrolled framework relies on these physical operators, a brief explanation of how the discrete projector is adapted on-the-fly would strengthen the paper.

Limited Unrolling Cascades: The framework is evaluated with only 3 cascades. In typical unrolled networks, using more cascades (e.g., 6–10) often leads to better performance. Clarifying whether the number of cascades was limited by memory/computational constraints of DISCO would be helpful.
